newsitem.title: UK: Copper - Shy upside, despite fundamental promise.
newsitem.headline: Copper - Shy upside, despite fundamental promise.

text.p: Copper prices stubbornly refuse to push significantly higher, despite a run of potentially constructive fundamental developments.

On the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Thursday news of a strike at Kennecott's 310,000 short ton a year smelter at Utah had only a muted impact.The plant, owned by RTZ-CRA, was struck on Wednesday, but prices edged up briefly, then settled back.
"Any sort of fundamental news does not have too much bearing in this market at present," said Martin Squires of LME broker Rudolf Wolff and Co.

Copper prices slipped subsequently to around $1,915 a tonne on Thursday, against Wednesday's $1,913. The market generally remains mired between $1,900 and $1,950 - a tight range within broader parameters of $1,880 and $1,970.
Some observers wondered whether RTZ-CRA was taking a tough line at Kennecott because the smelter has suffered from commissioning problems and has not operated to its full potential.
Consequently, Kennecott has built up significant stocks of concentrates - estimated to be above 70,000 tonnes - which are overhanging the spot treatment market.

Refined copper cathode inventories, meanwhile, have declined remorselessly in LME warehouses since the beginning of September, but again the market's response has been low key, as there are doubts whether copper is being consumed or re-located.
LME stocks now stand at 191,550 tonnes, the lowest since last October, having fallen nearly 85,000 tonnes in six weeks.
Analysts suggested that the copper inventory movement reflects a number of factors that are not as bullish as an initial reading of a stock drawdown indicates.
"Are all these withdrawals for consumption - that is the question," Peter Hollands of industry specialists Bloomsbury Minerals Economics said.
"The cards are being shuffled around, but the number in the deck remains basically the same," another analyst said.
In its daily review LME trader Brandeis said that arbitrage opportunities have being thrown up between the LME and markets in New York and Shanghai.
"The large premium that the Shanghai copper market commands over the LME (some $362/tonne) has seen shipments of copper moving from LME warehouses in Europe and the U.S. to China," Brandeis said.
Leading market trader Herbie Black, the President of American Iron and Metal Co, said last week that the Shanghai arbitrage was the next game in town.
He estimated that there are 140,000 tonnes of copper in Chinese warehouses that is off-warrant. Another 40,000 tonnes is being shipped there, he said.

If the metal, however much it is, is custom-cleared into China, then it will probably be consumed. But if it is being stored in bonded warehouses copper could easily return to the world market, Hollands said.
Montreal-based Black is widely believed to be one of those who broke Sumitomo Corp's grip on the copper market in May/June this year.
Copper plunged from a high point of $2,715 a tonne, with Sumitomo sacking its head trader Yasuo Hamanaka after it said that he had admitted 10 years of unauthorised trading.
The residue of Sumitomo's huge copper market positions may still be overhanging the market, and this is one of the factors preventing prices from breaking above $1,970, some traders said.
